rejected.title: Material and non-material living standards
card: Living standards
how well off people in a country are. They cover how much people can buy and also the quality of their lives.
Material
access to goods and services, such as food, housing, clothing, healthcare and transport. Income and consumption are common ways to measure it.
Non-material
things that are not bought or sold directly, such as a clean environment, good health, safety, literacy and leisure time.
Income can rise while non-material living standards fall. For example, a mining boom may lift incomes but add pollution to a town's air.
rejected.remember: Living standards include what people can buy and the quality of life around them.

a.q: Which of these is a change in non-material living standards?
opts: Cleaner air in a city after new pollution rules
A rise in the average wage of nurses
More new cars sold to households
A larger supply of rental housing
a.why: Cleaner air is part of the environment, which is not bought or sold directly, so it is non-material. The other three are about income or access to goods and services, which are material.
a.clue: Look for the change that is not about income or buying things.

b.q: Average income in the town of Kerang rises 10%, but workers now work much longer hours and have less leisure time. What is the effect on living standards?
opts: Material rises and non-material falls
Material and non-material both rise
Material falls and non-material rises
Material and non-material both fall
b.why: Higher income raises material living standards because people can buy more. Less leisure time is a non-material loss, so non-material living standards fall. Choosing both rise treats income as the whole picture and ignores the lost leisure time.
b.clue: Leisure time is on one side and income is on the other.
